item.title: Goldman sees upside risks (105 EUR!) to its 70 euro TTF gas forecast as Europe stocks run low
item.description:
Europe’s gas market is now tied directly to the same Gulf disruption that is driving crude, so escalation in the Middle East lifts both energy risk premia together. If Europe has to outbid other regions for LNG this winter, the strain falls hardest on price-sensitive importers in Asia and emerging markets, tightening the global market further. Higher gas prices also feed through to European power costs and industrial margins, adding to inflation pressure. The upside skew also strengthens the economic case for burning oil products instead of gas where switching is possible, a modest extra support for diesel and fuel oil demand.

---

Goldman’s base case still sees European gas easing to 70 euros, but low storage and shrinking Mideast LNG flows mean the risks point the other way.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says risks to its year-end TTF forecast of 70 euros per megawatt hour are skewed to the upside
  • Low European inventories and a month-on-month drop in Middle East LNG exports have supported TTF in the mid-80s
  • In a low-supply scenario with average weather, the bank estimates winter TTF would need to peak near 105 euros/MWh to cut enough LNG demand outside Europe
  • Goldman says uncertainty over winter weather widens the range of possible price outcomes further

Goldman Sachs sees the risks to its year-end forecast for European natural gas prices tilted to the upside, as low storage levels and falling Middle East LNG exports leave the region exposed heading into winter.

The bank’s forecast is for the Dutch TTF benchmark to stand at 70 euros per megawatt hour at the end of the year. That sits well below current levels, with Goldman noting that low inventories and a sequential drop in Middle East LNG exports have supported prices in the mid-80s. The gap implies the bank still expects some easing in its base case, but sees the balance of risks leaning towards higher prices.

At the centre of Goldman’s analysis is the question of how high prices would need to go to keep Europe supplied. In a scenario combining low supply with average winter weather, the bank estimates TTF would have to rally to a peak of around 105 euros/MWh. At that level, enough LNG demand elsewhere in the world would be priced out to free up cargoes for Europe. In practice, Europe would need to outbid other buyers, mainly in Asia, for a limited pool of seaborne gas.

Weather adds another layer of uncertainty. Goldman said uncertainty over winter conditions widens the range of possible outcomes further. A cold winter would accelerate storage withdrawals and intensify competition for cargoes, while a mild one would ease pressure on both inventories and prices.

The drop in Middle East LNG exports links the European gas market directly to the conflict in the region, which has already disrupted crude flows and shipping. Goldman’s assessment suggests gas traders will be watching Gulf export volumes and weather forecasts closely. With storage starting from a low base, Europe has less room to absorb either a supply shock or a cold snap than in a typical year, and the path of TTF this winter is likely to depend on how both develop.

Explainer: Understanding European gas pricing

TTF (Title Transfer Facility) The Dutch virtual trading hub for natural gas. TTF futures are Europe’s main benchmark for wholesale gas prices, much as Brent is for crude oil. When analysts quote “European gas prices,” they usually mean the front-month TTF contract.

EUR/MWh (euros per megawatt hour) The unit TTF is priced in. A megawatt hour measures the energy content of the gas, not its volume, so the price reflects the energy delivered. As a rough guide, a move from 70 to 85 euros/MWh is an increase of a little over 20% in the wholesale cost of that energy.

LNG (liquefied natural gas) Natural gas cooled to a liquid so it can be shipped by tanker. Europe relies heavily on LNG imports, which means it competes with buyers worldwide, particularly in Asia, for the same cargoes.

Demand destruction The point at which prices rise high enough that some buyers cut back or switch fuels. Goldman’s 105 euro estimate is the level at which enough buyers outside Europe would step back to leave sufficient LNG for European needs.

Injection and withdrawal seasons Europe typically injects gas into storage in the warmer months and draws it down over winter. Inventory levels going into winter are a key gauge of how well supplied the region is.

Sequential drop A decline compared with the previous period, here month-on-month, rather than year-on-year.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 13 Oct: Dollar retreats as traders await CPI; oil rises and stocks slip
item.description:
Tomorrow’s U.S. CPI report is the next big test for the markets. Will inflation remain concentrated in energy, or will the data show price pressures spreading more broadly? That question took on added importance after Susan Collins, president of the Boston Fed, reiterated her support for another rate hike before year-end.

Tuesday’s market moves were mixed. The dollar gave back ground against all the major currencies, longer-term Treasury yields moved lower, and stocks were modestly lower after a volatile session. Oil continued higher as Middle East tensions kept supply and shipping risks in focus. Existing-home sales beat expectations, but the report had little market impact.

Dollar gives back some ground

The dollar was lower across the major currencies in the late-session snapshot. Its largest decline was against the Canadian dollar, while its smallest decline was against the yen.

The currency levels showed:

  • EURUSD: 1.1196, +0.39%.

  • USDJPY: 158.30, −0.20%.

  • GBPUSD: 1.3251, +0.34%.

  • USDCHF: 0.8324, −0.24%.

  • USDCAD: 1.4213, −0.48%.

  • AUDUSD: 0.6981, +0.32%.

  • NZDUSD: 0.5611, +0.45%.

Higher oil provided a supportive backdrop for the Canadian dollar as did technicals (see post here).. More broadly, the dollar’s retreat reversed some of Monday’s strength as traders positioned ahead of CPI.

Longer-term Treasury yields ease

The late-session Treasury snapshot showed a modest rise in the 2-year yield, while longer maturities moved lower:

  • 2-year: 4.7974%, +0.64 basis points.

  • 5-year: 5.0085%, −1.25 basis points.

  • 10-year: 5.2168%, −2.72 basis points.

  • 30-year: 5.5660%, −3.33 basis points.

The curve flattened as longer-term yields fell more than short-term yields. The move offered some relief from elevated borrowing costs, but with the 10-year still above 5.2%, yields remain an important consideration for equities.

Stocks lower after a volatile session

The modest late-session declines hide a much wider trading range, particularly for the Dow. It was up 466.06 points at its high and down about 263 points at its low. The S&P and Nasdaq Composite also traded on both sides of unchanged. The Nasdaq 100 remained lower throughout the session.

The supplied late-session levels showed:

  • Dow industrial average: 51,675.16, −181.02 points or −0.35%.

  • S&P 500: 7,805.45, −1.79 points or −0.02%.

  • Nasdaq Composite: 27,204.38, −41.52 points or −0.15%.

  • Russell 2000: 2,783.37, −11.11 points or −0.40%.

  • Nasdaq 100: 30,569.48, −95.22 points or −0.31%.

Earnings begin, but buyers remain cautious

Earnings season got underway with reports from JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, Johnson & Johnson and UnitedHealth. In the earlier update, all six shares were trading lower.

The reactions underline that beating estimates alone does not guarantee a higher share price. Goldman Sachs beat both earnings and revenue expectations, while JPMorgan missed both. Traders also have to weigh guidance, valuations and the broader backdrop of higher energy costs and elevated interest rates.

European shares close mostly lower

European markets finished with small declines in most major indices, while Italy edged higher:

  • Germany’s DAX: 25,259.91, −0.07%.

  • France’s CAC 40: 7,827.64, −0.07%.

  • UK’s FTSE 100: 10,650.34, −0.06%.

  • Spain’s IBEX 35: 19,210.70, −0.39%.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: 50,057.17, +0.04%.

Collins focuses on the breadth of inflation

Susan Collins, president of the Boston Fed, said economic uncertainty is elevated and that she is watching how widespread inflation pressures become.

Her comments followed earlier remarks supporting another rate increase before the end of 2026. She highlighted AI and data-centre investment, tariffs and energy costs tied to the Middle East war as potential sources of persistent inflation.

For traders, the distinction matters. Higher gasoline prices can lift headline inflation directly. A broader rise in goods and services prices would suggest the pressure is becoming more entrenched—and give the Fed a stronger reason to tighten further. Collins’ comments kept that question front and centre ahead of CPI.

New York Fed President John Williams also spoke today and said one more rate hike is appropriate this year, but he currently sees no need for another increase in 2027. He expects inflation to slow considerably and approach the Fed’s 2% target next year, noting limited broader price pressures outside AI and energy and no signs that the labor market is fueling inflation.

The comments eased concerns about further tightening next year, helping push Treasury yields lower and extending the dollar’s losses. However, Williams did not signal rate cuts. His outlook remains dependent on inflation slowing as expected.

Home sales beat, but have little impact

September existing-home sales came in at an annualized rate of 3.99 million, above the 3.95 million estimate. Sales increased 1.5% month over month but remained 2.2% below a year earlier.

The South and West recorded monthly gains, the Midwest was unchanged, and the Northeast declined. Sales were lower year over year in all four regions.

Higher inventory and longer selling times are giving buyers more negotiating power, but rising mortgage rates remain a hurdle. The report offered a modest improvement in a still-soft housing market and did little to shift attention away from inflation and the Fed.

Oil rises as Middle East risks persist

Crude oil futures settled at $94.14, up $0.40 or 0.43%. The later supplied snapshot showed the CL1! contract trading at $94.93, up $1.19 or 1.27%.

Reports of discussions between President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about renewed action against Iran, threats to shipping near the Strait of Hormuz, and Saudi-led strikes against a Houthi-linked oil facility in Yemen kept escalation risks in focus.

The concern extends beyond oil supply. Sustained strength in fuel prices can raise transportation and production costs, keeping the broader inflation question alive.

Gold and silver fail to benefit from the weaker dollar

Spot gold was trading near $4,159.65, down $12.00 or 0.29%. Silver fell $1.164 to $59.1325, a decline of 1.93%.

A weaker dollar and lower longer-term yields would normally help gold. Tuesday’s decline shows those supportive moves were not enough to bring buyers in ahead of CPI. Silver’s larger fall also stood out, although the supplied data do not identify a specific catalyst.

Bitcoin rebounds

Bitcoin was trading at $83,314, up $1,568 or 1.92%.

The gain contrasted with softer equities and precious metals. The weaker dollar provided a supportive backdrop, but one session does not establish a lasting change in Bitcoin’s relationship with other risk assets.

CPI is the next shove

Wednesday’s September CPI report is due at 8:30 AM ET. InvestingLive’s preview points to headline inflation rising 0.6% month over month and about 3.7% year over year, with core inflation increasing around 0.2% monthly and holding near 2.4% annually.

The core reading and the breadth of price increases will be key. A firmer underlying number could revive expectations for an earlier Fed hike, while a softer reading would give policymakers more room to wait. Alongside CPI, traders will be watching oil, Middle East headlines and the next round of earnings.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morgan Stanley lifts Brent forecast to $105 as costly freight favours short-haul crude
item.description:
The freight argument points to Brent holding a firmer premium over long-haul grades, including WTI delivered into Europe, for as long as shipping stays expensive. Refiners in Northwest Europe benefit from cheaper delivered barrels from Brazil, West Africa and the US, while producers of those grades absorb the cost through weaker differentials. The main risk to the call is a sustained fall in freight rates, for example from a durable normalisation of Hormuz traffic, which would remove the Brent-specific support even if overall supply stays tight. Traders should watch tanker rates and physical differentials as closely as the flat price.

---

Earlier:

  • Catch up time! Oil settles mixed, Brent near $106; booms reported near Aramco HQ in Dhahran

---

Morgan Stanley says Brent’s $100-plus price is no longer only about missing barrels: the cost of shipping them is doing much of the work.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley raised its Brent forecast to $105 a barrel for 4Q26 from $100, and to $100 for 1Q27 from $95
  • The bank notes Persian Gulf crude exports are back within 10% of prewar levels, yet Brent remains above $100
  • It says supply, inventories and geopolitical risk all matter, but Brent gains specifically from being a short-haul crude while freight is unusually costly
  • Long-haul grades from Brazil, West Africa and US WTI shipped to Northwest Europe have seen their prices fall against Brent to partly absorb higher shipping costs
  • The move follows an August upgrade that lifted the 4Q26 forecast to $100 from $75, citing a slow Middle East supply recovery and falling inventories

Morgan Stanley has raised its Brent crude forecasts for a second time in less than two months, arguing that unusually expensive freight is giving the North Sea benchmark a specific advantage over competing crudes.

The bank now expects Brent to average $105 a barrel in the fourth quarter of 2026, up from $100, and $100 in the first quarter of 2027, up from $95. Its analysts note that Persian Gulf crude exports have recovered to within 10% of their prewar levels, yet Brent continues to trade above $100.

Morgan Stanley said supply, inventories and geopolitical risk all play a part in keeping prices high, but one factor works in Brent’s favour in particular. Brent is a short-haul crude, delivered mainly over short distances into European markets, at a time when shipping costs are well above normal. Long-haul alternatives have had to adjust instead. The bank said crudes from Brazil and West Africa, along with US West Texas Intermediate, shipped into Northwest Europe have seen their free-on-board prices fall relative to Brent as sellers partly absorb the higher cost of freight.

The latest revision builds on a sharp upgrade in late August, when the bank lifted its Brent forecasts from a flat $75 assumption to $90 for the third quarter of 2026, $100 for the fourth quarter, $95 for the first quarter of 2027 and $90 for the second quarter. At that stage, Morgan Stanley pointed to a slower than expected recovery in Middle East supply stretching well into 2027, a market in deficit through the turn of the year, and steep declines in both oil-on-water and onshore inventories, including in China. It also flagged a record gap between crude and refined products, with gasoil trading far above Brent.

The new note shifts the emphasis. With Gulf exports now largely restored, the bank’s case leans less on missing barrels and more on the cost and logistics of moving oil, a dynamic that particularly benefits Brent.

The outlook still depends heavily on how the Middle East conflict develops. Freight costs and shipping security through the Gulf are now central to whether Brent can hold above $100 into next year. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Catch up time! Oil settles mixed, Brent near $106; booms reported near Aramco HQ in Dhahran
item.description:
The deferred curve is carrying the bigger signal. WTI for calendar 2027 hit a record for a 12th straight session, around $84, and Brent’s 2027 strip set records on Monday near $90. That suggests the market is pricing a lasting supply deficit, not just a front-month war premium. Diesel remains the pressure point, with product strength outpacing crude and keeping refining margins elevated. With the Dhahran reports coming late in the day, the Asian open is the first real test of how much Aramco infrastructure risk gets priced back into Brent. A narrower Brent-WTI spread also points to Middle East risk being offset at the margin by the prospect of more Russian barrels.

---

I'm doing a bit of a catch up on crude if its of any use to anyone. 

Earlier:

  • Crude oil futures settle up $0.40 at $94.14

---

Oil is caught between a Russian diesel deal that promises more supply and a Saudi-Houthi war that now reaches the doorstep of Aramco’s headquarters.

Summary:

  • Brent settled down nearly $1, or circa 1%, at around $106, after Monday’s highest close since mid-September; WTI rose about 40 cents to around $94, its highest close since late September
  • Hopes the US-Russia diesel export deal could free up Russian supply offset Middle East risk; the Kremlin said the deal has no direct link to Ukraine peace talks
  • Loud booms were reported near Saudi Aramco’s Dhahran headquarters amid an escalating Saudi-Houthi war; Aramco did not comment
  • OPEC said OPEC+ output rose sharply in September, led by Saudi Arabia lifting crude production to around 8.4 million bpd from around 6.2 million in August
  • OPEC cut its 2026 demand growth forecast for a sixth straight month and raised next year’s outlook, citing the need to rebuild inventories depleted by the Iran war
  • Trump accused the Houthis of trying to drive up oil prices before the US midterm elections

Oil prices settled mixed on Tuesday as hopes that a US-Russia deal on diesel exports could release more supply from Moscow offset an escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis that threatens Gulf energy infrastructure.

Brent crude futures settled at around $106 a barrel, down nearly $1 or circa 1%, after closing on Monday at their highest level since mid-September. US West Texas Intermediate rose about 40 cents to settle at around $94, its strongest close since late September, Reuters reported.

The Kremlin said it saw no direct link between the diesel deal and its position on Ukraine peace talks. It was responding to a Reuters report that US President Donald Trump’s envoys had told Ukrainian officials the arrangement was part of an effort to bring Russia back to negotiations. Trump said the Russian diesel was destined for the rest of the world rather than the United States. US diesel futures still traded up circa 5%, a sign the market remains unconvinced the deal will ease tight product supply. Diesel prices have recently hit record highs in many regions after Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy sites and Iranian attacks on Middle East infrastructure.

In the Gulf, loud booms were heard on Tuesday night near Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, the centre of the kingdom’s oil industry, according to six sources cited by Reuters. One source said the building had been struck, though it was unclear whether by a direct hit or falling debris, and an evacuation order was issued, four sources said. Aramco did not comment. The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of an intercepted missile had fallen on a residential area.

Earlier, the coalition had targeted a Yemen Petroleum Company fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa, according to Houthi-run media, and the Houthis threatened Saudi oil facilities in response. The group has spent a week firing missiles and drones at Saudi targets, including Riyadh’s international airport. Trump accused the Houthis of deliberately trying to push up oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections and said he would make a decision on Iran very soon. Separately, reports said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had discussed with Trump last week the possibility of a joint operation against Iranian military and nuclear targets, a call that came before Trump said he would not strike Iran ahead of the midterms. Iranian authorities said a tanker they described as violating rules caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.

On the supply side, OPEC said OPEC+ production rose sharply in September, driven by Saudi Arabia lifting crude output to around 8.4 million barrels per day from around 6.2 million in August, despite continued disruption to Hormuz shipments. Around a fifth of global oil supply moved through the strait before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. OPEC also trimmed its 2026 demand growth forecast for a sixth consecutive month while raising its outlook for next year, citing the need to rebuild depleted inventories.

In a further sign of widening geopolitical strain, Britain’s domestic intelligence chief said Russia and Iran were stepping up hybrid warfare campaigns in the UK. With the Dhahran reports landing late in the session, traders will look to the Asian open for the first market verdict on the risk to Saudi infrastructure.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Collins says uncertainty is elevated as she watches breadth of inflation pressures
item.description:
Collins’ focus on how widespread inflation is moves attention to core and services prices, not just the headline energy-driven numbers. Signs of fuel costs spreading into broader prices would firm December hike pricing and support front-end yields and the dollar. For oil, that means sustained strength in crude and products now carries a second-round risk the Fed is explicitly watching. Her stress on elevated uncertainty also leaves room for the data to delay the next move, which caps how aggressively markets can price an October hike.

---

Collins has already called for another hike, and now she is spelling out what will set the timing: whether inflation spreads beyond energy in an uncertain economy.

Summary:

  • Boston Fed President Susan Collins said economic uncertainty is elevated
  • She is watching how broad inflation pressures are in the incoming data
  • Collins said she is very focused on inflation data and looks at the economy as a whole when considering rate policy
  • The comments follow her earlier remarks backing a further rate rise before the end of 2026
  • The Fed lifted its policy rate to 3.75%-4.00% in September, and several officials have pointed to December over October for the next move

Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins said on Tuesday that economic uncertainty is elevated and that she is paying close attention to how broad-based inflation pressures are, as she set out the factors that will shape her view on the timing of the next rate move.

Collins said she is very focused on the inflation data and that she looks at the economy holistically when weighing the future path of policy. Her emphasis on breadth suggests she will be watching whether price pressures spread into a wider range of goods and services, rather than staying concentrated in a few categories.

The comments add detail to remarks earlier in the day in which [Collins said she expects the Fed to raise rates again before the end of 2026]. In that speech text, prepared for a banking conference at the Boston Fed, she said she had supported the central bank’s quarter-point hike in September, which took the policy rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, and called the risk of high inflation the Fed’s main focus.

Collins has flagged several forces that could keep inflation above the Fed’s 2% target, including investment in data centres and artificial intelligence infrastructure, the ongoing effect of tariffs, and energy costs linked to the war in the Middle East. She has said she expects both headline and core inflation to run above target in coming months, citing recent increases in prices for refined fuels such as diesel, jet fuel and heating oil.

Her baseline outlook remains constructive, with healthy growth, a job market near full employment and a gradual return of inflation to target. Her latest comments make clear, however, that she sees the outlook as uncertain and that the incoming data will decide how quickly she wants policy to move.

Policymaker projections released in September pointed to one more increase this year. Several Fed officials have suggested in recent weeks that it is more likely in December than at the October 27-28 meeting, and Collins has said the policy path into the new year will depend on the data.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stocks close lower after volatile session
item.description:
US stocks closed lower Tuesday, but the closing changes tell only part of the story. The Dow swung through nearly 729 points, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite traded on both sides of unchanged. The Nasdaq 100 never made it into positive territory.

Earnings season got underway with JPMorgan, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, Johnson & Johnson and UnitedHealth reporting. The results were mixed, but the share-price reaction was consistent: all six finished lower. Even earnings beats and improved guidance were not enough to keep buyers in control.

Attention now turns to September’s US CPI report, due Wednesday at 8:30 AM ET. That gives traders another important test as they weigh corporate earnings against the inflation outlook.

That recovery helped limit the damage. It did not turn the session positive.

Earnings: the results and the reaction

  • JPMorgan Chase: missed earnings and revenue; shares fell 0.88%. EPS of $5.57 fell short of $5.93 expected, and revenue of $50.2 billion missed the $51.23 billion estimate.   • UnitedHealth: beat earnings and revenue, with guidance above expectations; shares still slipped 0.20%. Adjusted EPS of $4.69 exceeded $4.12 expected, and revenue of $112.7 billion topped $111.31 billion expected. Full-year adjusted EPS is projected at at least $20.50, versus $19.80 expected.

Chip shares struggle, but some technology names rally

Several semiconductor and related names were among the notable losers:

  • Applied Materials: down 6.69%.

  • Cadence Design Systems: down 4.08%.

  • Micron: down 3.65%.

  • KLA: down 3.22%.

  • SK hynix ADR: down 3.19%.

Caterpillar also fell 3.34%.

There were pockets of strength, however. Oracle and Meta moved higher, while Texas Instruments bucked the weakness in several chip-related peers.

Notable gainers included:

  • Oracle: up 4.28%.

  • First Solar: up 3.83%.

  • Deere: up 2.75%.

  • Meta Platforms: up 2.63%.

  • Shake Shack: up 2.57%.

  • CF Industries: up 2.31%.

Trading lesson: a beat is not a buy signal

Goldman Sachs and UnitedHealth beat earnings and revenue expectations, yet both closed lower. For a newer trader, that is a useful reminder: the headline result and the market reaction are two different things.

Watch whether buyers can hold the initial gains and sustain a move above resistance. If those gains disappear, the earnings beat alone is not enough confirmation. Today’s wide swings also show why the closing change can understate how much risk traders faced during the session.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - China inflation data
item.description:
China releases consumer and producer price data for September at 0130 GMT on Wednesday, which is 9:30 pm US Eastern time on Tuesday. Factory-gate inflation is the reading most likely to move markets, as higher global energy costs continue to feed through the economy.

August sets the benchmark. Consumer prices rose 0.8% y/y, up from 0.5% and in line with forecasts, while the 0.4% monthly gain beat expectations. Producer prices climbed 3.8% y/y from 3.5%, with the statistics bureau pointing to rising energy prices.

There are three things to watch.

  • The first is producer prices. The August increase reflected imported inflation, with higher crude oil and non-ferrous metal prices lifting petrochemical and smelting prices at home. Another firm print would confirm that the oil shock is still working its way through Chinese input costs.
  • The second is pass-through to consumers. Headline CPI remains well short of Beijing’s informal target of around 3%. Analysts warn that a weak property sector and soft consumption make it hard for downstream manufacturers to pass on higher costs, and that factory prices could slip back towards deflation once supply-side support fades. A widening gap between strong PPI and modest CPI would point to a squeeze on margins, not demand-led inflation.
  • The third is core CPI, which excludes food and energy. It gives the clearest read on whether domestic demand is firming or whether energy is doing all the work.

Trade figures for September are also on the calendar. In August, exports rose 18.6% y/y and imports 21.7% in yuan terms, with import growth outpacing exports for a sixth straight month. The dollar-denominated surplus was around $119 billion.

For markets, a hot PPI would add to signs that China is passing higher goods prices on to the rest of the world after years of exporting disinflation. A soft CPI would keep the focus on weak household demand and support the case for further policy easing.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Collins backs another rate hike by year-end, flags three inflation pressures
item.description:
Collins’ remarks reinforce expectations of another quarter-point rise before year-end, with recent Fed commentary leaning towards December rather than this month’s meeting. That should keep front-end Treasury yields supported and limit room for a sustained dollar pullback while hikes stay in play. For oil traders, the significance is the feedback loop: further gains in crude and refined products tied to the Middle East war now feed straight into Fed hike expectations, so energy strength carries rates and dollar consequences. A softer run of data would be the main thing to cool that pricing.

---

Earlier:

  • Fed Williams: Sees no need for rate hike in 2027 at this time

---

Collins sees a resilient economy as giving the Fed licence to keep tightening, with war-driven fuel costs the clearest reason inflation won’t get back to target on its own.

Summary:

  • Boston Fed President Susan Collins expects a further rate increase to be appropriate before the end of 2026
  • She supported last month’s quarter-point hike that took the policy rate to 3.75%-4.00%
  • Collins called the risk of high inflation elevated and the Fed’s main focus, with inflation above target for more than five years
  • Her baseline sees healthy growth, a broadly balanced job market near full employment and a gradual return of inflation to 2%
  • She flagged data-centre and AI investment, tariffs and Middle East war-driven energy costs as risks, expecting headline and core inflation above target in coming months
  • Timing of the next move depends on data; several officials have signalled December rather than the October 27-28 meeting

Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins said on Tuesday she expects the US central bank will need to lift interest rates again before the end of 2026, arguing that further tightening is needed to return inflation to the Fed’s 2% target in a timely and lasting way.

In prepared remarks for a banking conference at the Boston Fed, reported by Reuters, Collins said she had supported the Federal Open Market Committee’s decision last month to raise its policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%. She indicated that a modest additional increase would likely be appropriate this year, while stressing that her view on both the need for and timing of further action would rest on the full body of incoming data and how it shapes the balance of risks.

Collins framed the inflation fight as the Fed’s central task. With growth holding up and the labour market broadly balanced, she said policymakers have room to concentrate on bringing inflation back to target, a goal the Fed has now missed for more than five years. She described the risk of persistently high inflation as elevated and the central bank’s main focus at present.

Her baseline outlook was largely constructive. In what she called the most likely scenario, the economy keeps growing at a healthy pace, the job market stays close to full employment and inflation eases gradually back to 2%, helped by ongoing efficiency gains that keep supply and demand in balance. She added that a stable labour market should continue to underpin consumer spending.

Collins nonetheless identified three forces that could complicate that path: heavy investment in data centres and other artificial intelligence infrastructure, the continuing effect of tariffs, and higher energy costs linked to the war in the Middle East. She said she expects both headline and core inflation to run above target again in the coming months, pointing to the recent jump in prices for refined products such as jet fuel, diesel and heating oil.

Projections published at the September meeting already pencilled in another increase before year-end. Several Fed officials have signalled in recent weeks that the move is more likely to come in December than at the October 27-28 meeting, and Collins’ comments keep a further hike firmly on the table while leaving its timing open. She said the policy path into the new year would depend on the data.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US CPI: Energy prices expected to lift headline inflation. Will core stay contained?
item.description:
The US CPI report for September will be released tomorrow at 8:30 AM ET. The report - along with the PPI on Thursday - will give traders another key piece of the inflation puzzle as markets assess whether the Fed will need to tighten policy further. Number crunchers will also be able to get a handle on the PCE and Core PCE from both readings. 

The expectations are seeing: 

  • Headline CPI month over month: +0.6% expected versus +0.4% last month.

  • Headline CPI year over year: +3.6% expected versus +3.4% last month.

  • Core CPI month over month: +0.2% expected versus +0.3% last month.

  • Core CPI year over year: +2.5% expected versus +2.4% last month.

The core numbers will be the focus.  A 0.1% MoM (or better) core and 2.4% (or better) YoY would be moving in the right direction. . 

The key question: How far are energy costs spreading?

Higher energy prices are expected to drive the stronger headline reading.

The more important question for the broader inflation outlook is whether those costs are filtering into other goods and services. That puts the core reading—which excludes food and energy—firmly in focus.

Last month, gasoline prices rose 3.9%, accounting for more than one-third of the monthly headline increase. However, core prices also rose 0.3%, with increases in categories including airline fares, lodging and used vehicles. Traders will be watching whether those underlying pressures ease in September.

A 0.2% monthly core reading would represent a slowdown from August, even if the annual rate edges higher. Those two measures can move in different directions because the annual comparison also depends on the reading from a year ago.

What could it mean for markets?

My read is that the core surprise will be an important driver of the reaction:

  • Hotter core inflation: A reading of 0.3% or higher could lift Treasury yields and support the dollar as traders reassess the risk of further Fed tightening. I am leaning that a October hike - although it may be needed - is odds on a no go for political purposes. The Fed will let the market do the tightening for them and remain out of the hot seat (it is just the way it is with Trump as President).  

  • Core in line at 0.2%: That could give the Fed more room to wait, particularly if the headline increase is concentrated in energy.

  • Softer core inflation: A reading of 0.1% or lower could pressure yields and the dollar and provide some relief for stocks. Although December may still be on the table (one more hike), the chance for October works closer toward 0% from about 20% currently.  

For currency traders, the data will provide the shove. The technical levels will help tell us whether buyers or sellers can keep control after that initial move.

Watch where the price trades relative to the pre-release range, nearby swing levels and the 100- and 200-hour moving averages. A break that holds carries more weight. A break that quickly reverses tells us the market had its shot—and could not follow through.

item.title: USDCAD sellers regain control, but key swing support stands in the way
item.description:
The USDCAD extended to a new high for the year on Friday following the weaker-than-expected Canadian jobs report. However, the breakout could only stretch about 7 pips above the previous yearly high near 1.4292 before reversing lower.

The buyers had their shot. They could not keep the break going.

By Friday’s close, the price had rotated lower. Selling continued on Monday until the pair reached its rising 100- and 200-hour moving averages—the blue and green lines on the chart. Buyers leaned against those levels and pushed the price higher.

That rebound stalled near Monday’s closing level and below the previous yearly high at 1.4292. Today, sellers have taken back control, pushing the pair lower in a more trend-like move. The USDCAD is down about 0.48%, making the Canadian dollar the strongest performer against the US dollar.

Sellers reach the next downside hurdle

The decline has reached the top of a swing area between 1.41922 and 1.4204. That area is defined by swing highs and lows going back to September 29, highlighted by the red numbered circles on the chart.

So far, the price has stalled near the upper boundary at 1.4204.

Sellers have secured a victory with the move below the hourly moving averages. To increase their control, however, they need to break below this swing area and stay below it. That would open the door for further downside momentum toward the next swing area between 1.41297 and 1.4153.

Can buyers defend support again?

If buyers hold this area for a fourth consecutive test, the focus shifts toward a rebound to the 100- and 200-hour moving averages near 1.4250.

Those moving averages become the next upside hurdle. Getting above—and staying above—them would weaken the sellers’ control and bring the yearly high near 1.4298 back into focus.

For now, sellers are enjoying the victory today, but they still have work to do. The 1.41922–1.4204 swing area is where their next test begins.

The trading lesson

A break below the moving averages shifts the short-term bias, but the next support area still matters. Sellers need to see follow-through. Buyers need to see support hold.

Use the swing area to define risk and judge control. Hold support, and buyers have a reason to lean against it. Break below and stay below, and sellers earn another victory.

item.title: Stock market movers today. Bumble, JPMorgan and AI stocks: Why market reactions reversed
item.description:
Stocks reverse after the market opens: Bumble's deal, bank earnings and the AI-chip selloff

October 13, 2026 | U.S. stocks | Market snapshot: 10:35 a.m. ET, using 15-minute-delayed data

A stock can rise on disappointing earnings, fall after encouraging guidance or change direction within minutes of the opening bell. Tuesday's U.S. session illustrates why traders should look beyond the first headline. Bumble's takeover, JPMorgan's earnings recovery, healthcare weakness and a selloff in AI-related hardware all offer different lessons about how markets price expectations.

The common thread is that a news event explains why investors are paying attention, but subsequent price action helps reveal how they are evaluating that news.

1. Bumble stock: when a takeover rumor becomes a confirmed offer

Bumble (BMBL) offers perhaps the clearest example of how a trading opportunity can change overnight.

On Monday, shares of the dating-app company surged nearly 50% following reports that it was discussing a potential take-private transaction.

On Tuesday, speculation became an announced agreement. Ithaca Holdings agreed to acquire Bumble in an all-cash transaction valued at approximately $1.3 billion, offering shareholders $6.05 per share.

Bumble shares traded near $5.95 in the supplied morning snapshot, approximately 56.5% above Monday's close.

But the educational opportunity is not simply another large percentage gain.

It is understanding how the nature of the investment changes once an acquisition price becomes public.

At $5.945, the stock was trading approximately 1.77% below the announced cash consideration.

Why would anyone sell at $5.945 when the proposed buyer is offering $6.05?

Because $6.05 is conditional on completing the transaction. Investors must consider the closing timetable, regulatory and other conditions, the opportunity cost of tying up capital, and the possibility that the deal fails.

That difference is called the merger arbitrage spread. It represents potential gross compensation for assuming the time and risk involved, not a guaranteed return.

What to watch:Transaction documents, closing conditions, expected completion timing and any changes to the agreement. A widening spread could reflect greater perceived risk, a longer expected wait or broader market conditions.

The lesson: A stock trading below an agreed takeover price is not automatically undervalued.

2. JPMorgan: why a disappointing earnings report did not keep shares down

JPMorgan Chase (JPM) reported third-quarter net income of approximately $15.3 billion, with earnings of $5.57 per share against analysts' expectations near $5.93.

Reported revenue was approximately $50.2 billion, below the consensus estimate of $51.23 billion. The bank also disclosed $5.75 in earnings per share excluding a significant item, adding nuance to the headline miss.

The stock initially showed weakness.

An earlier 6:45 a.m. ET premarket observation placed JPM near $324.33, almost 3% below Monday's closing price of $334.30. That particular observation should not automatically be attributed to the earnings announcement without confirming the release timing.

During the regular session, the picture changed.

JPM traded above $344 shortly after the opening bell before retreating to approximately $335.78 by the supplied 10:35 a.m. snapshot. That still represented a gain of around 0.44% against Monday's close.

This raises a useful question: Why might investors buy a stock after an earnings miss?

One possibility is that the market distinguishes between a disappointing headline and the underlying operating performance. Investors may examine whether a shortfall reflects temporary trading conditions, unusual charges or more persistent business weakness.

Another possibility is that the initial selling pressure was excessive relative to what the report ultimately revealed.

Neither explanation can be established from the price reversal alone.

The wider banking sector reinforces the need to examine individual companies.

Goldman Sachs (GS):Shares gained approximately 1.55% in the supplied snapshot after the bank reported EPS of $17.01 and revenue of $18.68 billion.

Wells Fargo (WFC):Shares declined approximately 2.49%, despite the broader banking earnings season showing resilience.

JPMorgan (JPM):After moving from weakness to a modest gain, the bank offers a particularly interesting example of intraday reassessment.

The lesson: An earnings beat or miss is only one part of the story. Expectations, earnings quality and subsequent investor demand can matter just as much.

3. UnitedHealth and Johnson & Johnson: why improving fundamentals can accompany falling shares

Two major healthcare companies illustrate another important distinction.

An earnings report can contain genuinely encouraging information without producing a positive stock-market reaction.

UnitedHealth: better medical-cost control, but a fading initial reaction

UnitedHealth (UNH) reported adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share and raised its full-year adjusted earnings outlook to at least $20.50 per share.

Its medical-cost ratio improved to 88.4%, indicating that medical expenses were consuming a smaller share of premium revenue.

This is meaningful because controlling medical expenses is central to an insurer's profitability. Nevertheless, in the supplied morning price snapshot, UNH had reversed an earlier positive premarket response and was trading near $376.40, approximately 0.56% below Monday's close.

There are several possible explanations for such behavior.

Investors might welcome improved cost control while remaining uncertain about future insurance membership, pricing, the performance of Optum or the sustainability of the recovery.

A strong quarterly result does not remove every concern about the next several quarters.

Johnson & Johnson: the difference between reported and adjusted earnings

Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) reported third-quarter revenue of $25.4 billion, representing 5.9% growth, and raised its 2026 guidance.

Yet its financial results also illustrated why investors need to understand the difference between reported and adjusted earnings.

Reported EPS was just $0.09, compared with adjusted EPS of $2.59. Special charges included expenses associated with the proposed talc-litigation resolution and business-development transactions.

JNJ shares were down approximately 4.81% in the supplied snapshot.

Investors also had reason to examine the performance of the company's medical-technology division, where growth and competitive pressures remain important considerations.

These two healthcare companies offer a broader lesson.

Good news is not the same as news that exceeds expectations.

A company can improve operationally while its shares decline if investors were anticipating even better performance or believe future risks remain inadequately addressed.

4. Micron and storage stocks: the AI trade faces a competitive test

The pressure on memory and storage shares deserves attention because it has involved several companies rather than one isolated stock.

In the supplied morning snapshot:

Supplied 10:35 a.m. ET snapshot. Percentage changes are relative to the previous regular-session close, not final daily returns.

One reported catalyst is technological progress at Chinese memory producer ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT.

Reports indicate that CXMT has made advances in denser DRAM memory architecture, potentially improving its ability to compete with established global manufacturers.

DRAM is the short-term working memory used by computers and servers. Improvements in chip density can eventually influence production economics and competition.

However, an important distinction is getting lost when these developments are treated as proof that established memory companies are already losing business.

A technological advance is not the same as verified commercial displacement.

Before drawing that conclusion, investors would need evidence of competitive production costs, successful customer qualification, manufacturing yields, shipment volumes and actual changes in pricing.

There is also an important distinction between Micron and the storage companies.

Micron is primarily exposed to semiconductor memory markets, while Western Digital and Seagate have substantial exposure to hard-disk storage. Their products, competitors and pricing cycles are not identical.

What connects them is their exposure to data infrastructure investment and expectations around AI-related demand.

A selloff can weaken without becoming a recovery

Western Digital and Seagate had both recovered noticeably from their opening lows in the supplied snapshot, even though they remained negative for the session.

This is worth observing.

A stock that falls sharply at the open and then recovers part of its decline is behaving differently from one that continues making fresh lows.

But that improvement does not establish a durable bottom.

What to watch:Whether the shares continue recovering toward their previous closes or whether sellers regain control later in the session.

For longer-term investors, the more consequential questions involve memory and storage demand, capacity expansion, margins, competitive pricing and future free cash flow.

The lesson: Industry-wide selling can be informative, but the underlying businesses still require separate analysis.

5. Microsoft and Meta: the AI trade is not moving in one direction

Not all technology stocks were participating in the weakness.

In the supplied snapshot, Microsoft (MSFT) gained approximately 1.31%, while Meta Platforms (META) advanced approximately 3.33%.

Both were outperforming the Nasdaq-100 ETF, while Micron and several storage companies were moving in the opposite direction.

That divergence suggests investors were not treating every AI-exposed business identically.

One possible interpretation is that investors were differentiating between companies monetizing software, advertising and digital services and hardware businesses exposed to manufacturing cycles, capacity expansion and changing competitive conditions.

However, the distinction should not be overstated.

Microsoft and Meta also spend heavily on AI infrastructure, and the relationship between capital investment and eventual profitability is relevant to their valuations.

A single morning's relative performance does not establish a sustained rotation.

The useful question is whether this divergence persists over several sessions and is supported by business developments, or whether it proves to be temporary positioning.

For traders, relative strength can help identify which stocks are holding up better during broader market weakness.

For investors, it is only the beginning of the analysis. Business quality, valuation and expected cash generation still matter.

What traders should watch during the rest of Tuesday's session

Rather than trying to predict every stock's next move, traders can use the previous closing price as an initial reference for evaluating whether the market is accepting or rejecting the latest news.

JPM

$334.30

JPMorgan: Can the recovery survive?

Sustained trading above Monday's close would keep the recovery intact relative to that reference. A renewed move below it would weaken the immediate interpretation.

UNH

$378.52

UnitedHealth: Can buyers restore the positive reaction?

A recovery above the previous close would improve the immediate picture, while continued weakness would suggest investors remain unconvinced.

MU

$989.04

Micron: Is the semiconductor selloff stabilizing?

Watch whether buyers can recover some of the decline and whether the broader semiconductor sector participates.

WDC / STX

$386.94 / $753.25

Western Digital and Seagate: Can the rebounds develop?

A recovery toward their respective Monday closes would indicate improving price action, but sustained demand matters more than a brief bounce.

BMBL

$6.05

Bumble: The acquisition price is the key reference

Unlike the other stocks, the central question is whether the agreed transaction closes, rather than whether a normal earnings-driven price recovery continues.

All reference levels above are supplied October 12, 2026, regular-session closes, except Bumble's announced acquisition consideration. They are analytical reference points, not recommended entries, targets or stop-loss orders.

There is an important difference between the time horizons here.

A day trader may find a recovery above the previous close useful for assessing intraday demand. A longer-term investor should not mistake that recovery for confirmation that a company's business outlook or valuation has improved.

The reverse is also true. One difficult session does not necessarily undermine a sound long-term investment case.

The bigger lesson: markets trade expectations, not headlines

Tuesday's action reminds us that a stock's price reaction depends on more than the apparent quality of the news.

JPMorgan's recovery suggests that investors were willing to reconsider its earnings miss. UnitedHealth and Johnson & Johnson illustrate why stronger guidance or encouraging operational results may still fail to satisfy expectations.

Micron and the storage companies show how competitive developments can trigger concern across an industry, even before their full commercial consequences are known.

And Bumble illustrates something different again: once a takeover price is announced, the investment question changes from speculation about an offer to assessing the transaction's completion risk.

The opening price is information. It is not necessarily the market's final judgment.

For traders, watching how price behaves after the opening reaction can reveal whether that response is strengthening, weakening or being reversed.

For investors, those moves can identify questions worth investigating, but they should be considered alongside fundamentals, valuation and business risk.

Interest rates, bond yields and financing costs are among the forces influencing stock valuations and corporate investment decisions.

For a useful introduction to one of those building blocks, watch Filip explain "What is a bond?" in this short investingLive educational video.

Educational analysis only, not investment advice.

item.title: Crude oil futures rebound and pushed back into positive territory

Buyers reclaim $93.48. Yesterday’s high is next.

The rebound has taken the price back above the top of a swing area at $93.48, with crude currently trading near $93.79. Staying above $93.48 would keep the immediate momentum tilted higher.

Trading lesson: Use technical levels to define risk

When a Fibonacci retracement and moving averages sit close together, they create a cluster of support. That gives traders a clear area to judge whether buyers are holding control or sellers are gaining ground.

For crude oil, that area runs from $91.60 down to $90.86. Holding above it supports the bullish bias. Breaking below it—and staying below—would strengthen the sellers’ case.

Prices declined in all four regions during September. Compared with last year, the Northeast recorded the strongest increase, while the West was the only region with lower prices. These price figures are not seasonally adjusted, so monthly declines can reflect normal seasonal patterns.

September existing-home sales by region — seasonally adjusted annualized rates:

  • Northeast: 470,000 vs 480,000 in August, down 2.1% MoM. Down 4.1% YoY from 490,000 last September.
  • Midwest: 930,000 vs 930,000 in August, unchanged MoM. Down 2.1% YoY from 950,000.
  • South: 1.86 million vs 1.81 million in August, up 2.8% MoM. Down 0.5% YoY from 1.87 million.
  • West: 730,000 vs 710,000 in August, up 2.8% MoM. Down 5.2% YoY from 770,000.
  • National: 3.99 million vs 3.93 million in August, up 1.5% MoM. Down 2.2% YoY from 4.08 million.

The South and West drove September’s monthly gain. However, sales remained below last September in every region, with the West recording the largest annual decline.

Annualized means the monthly sales pace is expressed as a yearly rate, after adjusting for seasonal patterns. It is not the actual number of homes sold during the year.

US existing-home sales increased 1.5% in September, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). The gain offers some encouragement, but the broader picture remains soft. August and September were the two slowest months for sales this year on a seasonally adjusted basis.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said recent increases in mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to qualify. Meanwhile, higher inventory and longer selling times mean sellers may need to offer price discounts or other incentives. Buyers have more negotiating power, but financing remains a hurdle.

Quick analysis:Sales moved higher, but one monthly gain does not establish a recovery. Annual declines across all four regions point to continued weakness. Softer housing demand could weigh on growth and support lower yields at the margin, although this report alone is unlikely to change the Federal Reserve’s policy outlook.

What this report measures:Existing-home sales track completed purchases of previously owned homes, including single-family houses, condominiums and co-ops. The headline sales level is seasonally adjusted and annualized, meaning it expresses the monthly pace as a yearly rate. Traders watch the report for clues about housing demand and the impact of mortgage rates.

item.title: Gold rebounds after the run to the 100 and 200 hour MAs found buyers
item.description:
Yesterday, I did a post-on gold sellers on the back of news Kazakhstan was selling some of the reserves. I spoke cautiously in regard to the move given the semi-holiday trading, but acknowledged that the precious metal was testing a key target near the 100 and 200 hour moving averages and that the area would help define the next move.

See the post and the video HERE

Gold buyers ended up defending the  important technical area. The price has bounced higher in trading here today but those buyers still have work to do before claiming more control.

The pullback tested the 100-hour and 200-hour moving averages (blue and green lines on the chart below), where willing buyers helped stall the decline. The price has since bounced above those levels and is trading near $4,184 in the supplied chart. That is good news for the buyers. The next challenge is getting above and staying above the resistance overhead.

Hourly moving averages define the risk

The two hourly moving averages are nearly on top of each other:

  • 100-hour moving average: $4,157.82
  • 200-hour moving average: $4,157.78

That makes the area near $4,158 the immediate support barometer. Stay above, and buyers keep the recovery alive. It also gives traders a level where risk can be defined and limited.

Move below and stay below, however, and the support defense loses its significance. Sellers would regain more control, with attention turning back toward the recent lows.

Buyers still face an important ceiling

On the topside, the next key hurdle is the swing area between $4,223.51 and $4,237.55. That area has acted as both support and resistance on a number of occasions going back to June.

The 61.8% retracement at $4,229.43 sits inside that zone, adding another technical reason to pay attention when the price gets there.

Buyers have defended support, but they have not broken the ceiling. Getting above and staying above the swing area would be a more meaningful step toward stronger upside control.

Just above that zone is the 100-day moving average at $4,252.80. Buyers need to clear that level as well to strengthen the broader recovery. If they succeed, the next target would be the 50% retracement at $4,318.18.

Conversely, if sellers lean against those resistance levels and the price rotates lower, the rally would remain a recovery within the larger decline from the late-August high.

Trading education: Holding support is step one

This setup illustrates why traders should separate a successful support test from a confirmed change in the broader bias.

Holding the hourly moving averages tells us buyers are willing to defend that area. It does not automatically tell us they can overcome the sellers waiting above.

The sequence is straightforward:

  • Hold above the hourly moving averages to preserve the recovery.
  • Clear the swing area to overcome a repeatedly tested ceiling.
  • Get above and stay above the 100-day moving average to strengthen the bullish bias.

A brief move through resistance is only the first step. If the price cannot stay above it, sellers have a reason to lean against the level again. The follow-through matters.

For now, support near $4,158 keeps buyers in the near-term battle, while $4,223.51–$4,237.55 and $4,252.80 remain the upside hurdles. The price action will provide the next clue.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin sellers had a go but could not push the lower targets
item.description:
Bitcoin moved lower yesterday, breaking below its 100-hour moving average and approaching the bottom of the swing area at $81,183. The low reached $81,388, falling short of that key downside target before buyers stepped back in.

Sellers had their shot. They missed.

The rebound subsequently carried the price above the 100-hour moving average at $82,997 and the 200-hour moving average at $83,545. However, buyers could not sustain the upside momentum. The price has since slipped back between those two technical levels.

Moving averages become the barometers

With bitcoin sandwiched between the hourly moving averages, traders have clear levels to define risk and judge who is taking control:

  • Above the 200-hour MA at $83,545: The bias becomes more bullish. Buyers would then look toward resistance near $84,236, corresponding with Monday’s high and today’s high area. Getting above—and staying above—that level would give the rebound more credibility.

  • Below the 100-hour MA at $82,997: The bias shifts back toward the sellers. The downside focus returns to yesterday’s low at $81,388 and the swing-area floor at $81,183. Below that, the September 19 low at $80,106 becomes the next key target.

For beginner traders, the distinction is between crossing a moving average and holding beyond it. Today’s rebound crossed both averages, but the failure to stay above the 200-hour MA shows that buyers still have work to do.

The broader range still needs a shove

Bitcoin has been trading up and down within a broader range since September 18. The key boundaries remain $80,106 on the downside and $87,374 on the upside.

A sustained break beyond either extreme would signal that the market is finally resolving that consolidation. Until then, the 100- and 200-hour moving averages act as the nearer-term barometers within the range.

The sellers failed to reach their downside target. The buyers have responded, but have yet to establish control.

Be patient. Listen to the price action and the clues from the technical tools. Then wait for the next shove.

Trading lesson: A failed move creates an opportunity, but confirmation still matters

When sellers push toward support but cannot break through, traders should pay attention. That failure can trigger a rebound as sellers exit and buyers step in. However, a bounce alone does not mean buyers are in control.

That is where the moving averages help:

  • Stay above the 200-hour MA at $83,545: Buyers have a stronger case for further upside.

  • Move back below the 100-hour MA at $82,997: The rebound loses credibility, and sellers regain the advantage.

  • Remain between the averages: The market is still deciding. Be patient and wait for the next shove.

The lesson is to use technical levels to define your risk, judge the bias, and recognize when your trade idea is no longer working. You do not need to predict every move. You need to know what the price must do to support your view—and what would tell you that you are wrong.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Is the AI bubble bursting?
item.description:
Nostradamus has been dead for centuries, but his followers are still around, especially in finance, with Ray Dalio warning that the AI bubble may be close to bursting as interest rates rise and tech companies take on massive debt to build AI infrastructure.

Are we heading for another dot-com crash?

Things do seem to be getting murkier for the sector, with OpenAI’s annualized revenue reaching around $50 billion at the end of September, $20 billion below the previously expected $70 billion. As concerns grow that AI demand may be slowing and revenues may not justify massive infrastructure investments, Oracle, Microsoft, and Nvidia shares, alongside the Nasdaq-100, have naturally come under pressure. 

This week, selling pressure also spread to semiconductor and tech stocks across Asian markets. Chinese chipmaker CXMT’s progress in developing a new memory architecture has raised concerns about growing competition for global memory makers. On top of that, Broadcom’s CEO compared AI investors to casino gamblers, suggesting some don’t fully understand what they’re betting on, and warned that financing AI infrastructure could become a major challenge.

Looking ahead, high Treasury yields could add fuel to the fire by making riskier AI stocks less attractive to investors. 

Still, this isn’t a classic bubble, as massive infrastructure spending is backed by real growth in revenue, orders, and contract backlogs. Microsoft’s Azure, for example, has surpassed $100 billion in annual revenue, AWS has posted its fastest growth in years, and Celestica and AMD are also seeing strong demand for AI infrastructure. 

In other words, unlike in a typical bubble, companies aren’t betting on demand that may never materialize. They’re trying to keep up with demand that already exceeds capacity. At the same time, tech giants remain highly profitable and have ample cash to fund record investments without seriously risking their financial stability.

Still, the risks remain, as these massive investments have yet to pay off and high valuations — exceeding $2 trillion in the case of the upcoming Anthropic IPO — leave the sector vulnerable to growth disappointments, making this an important factor to consider when shaping your investment strategy. 

The next big test for the sector will be earnings season. By the way, this week, besides JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, Citigroup, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley, and BlackRock, ASML and TSMC will also report, giving us a better idea of whether the AI boom still has legs. 

This article was written by IL Contributors at investinglive.com.

The dollar is lower across the major currencies

The US earnings season is kicking off today with the traditional financials leading the way.  Goldman, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo have released along with J&J and UnitedHealth:

  • Goldman Sachs — beat earnings and revenue. EPS of $17.01 exceeded $13.07 expected. Revenue of $18.7 billion topped the $16.84 billion estimate.

However, the bank raised its full-year net interest income outlook to $106.2 billion, above both the previous $105.5 billion guidance and the $105.28 billion estimate.

  • UnitedHealth — beat earnings and revenue, with guidance above expectations. Adjusted EPS of $4.69 exceeded $4.12 expected. Revenue of $112.7 billion topped $111.31 billion expected. Full-year adjusted EPS is now projected at at least $20.50, versus $19.80 expected.

The lesson for traders is to look beyond the headline EPS number. Revenue, lending income and forward guidance can change how investors interpret a beat or a miss.

Korean chipmakers lead a sharp selloff

  • South Korea’s Kospi fell 5.46%.

The selling centered on the country’s semiconductor heavyweights:

  • Samsung Electronics: down approximately 7.4%.

  • SK Hynix: down approximately 10.1%.

Reports of advances at Chinese memory-chip producer CXMT raised concerns about competition for Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron. That added to broader unease over the AI investment boom. The Kospi recovered some ground after falling more than 7% intraday.

For the chipmakers, the concern is what increased competition could mean for pricing power and profit margins. Strong demand can continue, but investors also need confidence that the companies can maintain the earnings that support their valuations.

Treasury yields move lower

U.S. Treasury yields are lower as cash bond trading resumes:

  • 2-year:4.770%, down approximately 2.1 basis points.

  • 5-year:4.974%, down approximately 4.7 basis points.

  • 10-year:5.187%, down approximately 5.7 basis points.

  • 30-year:5.551%, down approximately 5.4 basis points.

The pullback in yields accompanies the softer dollar, but the 10-year remains above 5%. Tomorrow’s inflation report will be an important test of whether yields can continue to ease.

Fed commentary: AI spending and inflation

Austan, president of the Chicago Fed, warned that inflation remains too high and that AI-related demand may be spreading price pressures beyond data centers and their immediate suppliers. He described employment and consumer spending as solid, while expressing concern about broader overheating demand.

Christopher, a Fed governor, said the U.S. remains dominant in building AI models and that hyperscalers still plan substantial investment over the next three years. He also said higher yields could do some of the Fed’s work by restraining demand.

The policy question is whether AI investment raises productive capacity quickly enough to offset the demand and cost pressures created during the buildout.

RBA minutes keep further hikes on the table

The RBA’s September meeting minutes showed unanimous agreement that a 25-basis-point hike was necessary, taking the cash rate to 4.60%.

The board was concerned that excess demand was greater than previously assumed and that inflation could remain elevated. Higher oil prices, domestic cost pressures and signs of AI-related price pressures were among the concerns. The RBA reiterated that it would raise rates further if needed.

There is also evidence of strain. Australian business confidence fell to -13 in September, while business conditions held at -1. That leaves the RBA balancing weak confidence against persistent inflation pressures.

Oil and the Middle East remain key drivers

Oil is lower this morning, but the underlying geopolitical risks remain. Saudi Arabia has vowed a response to Houthi attacks, while U.S.-Iran negotiations remain stalled. Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure have added another source of uncertainty.

Saudi Arabia is also examining ways to increase its ability to move crude through pipelines. Converting a gas pipeline could add approximately 1.2 million barrels per day of capacity within seven to eight weeks, according to the Saudi energy minister. That could ease some transport concerns, although execution and security risks remain.

For markets, oil matters through the inflation channel. Renewed gains could keep pressure on yields and rate expectations. A sustained retreat would ease some of that pressure.

The calendar: Fed speakers today, CPI tomorrow

Today’s scheduled events include:

The bigger scheduled economic risk is Wednesday’s U.S. CPI report, with PPI and retail sales also ahead this week. Those reports will help traders assess inflation pressures and the strength of consumer demand.

The session high at 1.1196 is the immediate upside reference and is also near its 100 hour MA at 1.1193 currently. A break above it, followed by an ability to stay above, would give the rebound more momentum with the 200 hour MA at 1.1216 the next key target to get to and through. .

On the downside, 1.1154 is the session’s lower boundary. Buyers need to show they can hold higher levels rather than allow the rebound to unwind.

A break below 157.84 would extend the session’s dollar weakness. Failure to break and hold below that level would leave room for a rebound within the range.

The session high at 158.66 remains the upper reference for today’s trading.
